Cordell Hull. Secretary of State under President Franklin D. Roosevelt from 1933 to 1944, making him the longest-serving Secretary of State in American history. A devoted internationalist, Hull championed free trade, multilateral cooperation, and the nascent United Nations, working to navigate the treacherous waters of the Great Depression and World War Two while attempting to keep the United States on a path toward peace and democratic collective action.

Hull served as Secretary of State for twelve years, from 1933 to 1944, the longest tenure of any person in that office. During those years, he negotiated Reciprocal Trade Agreements, reducing tariffs and promoting free trade during a time when isolationism was strong throughout America.

He championed the Good Neighbor Policy toward Latin America, renouncing interventionism and strengthening hemispheric ties. This represented a major shift in American approach to the Western Hemisphere. Throughout the 1930s and into the war years, Hull pushed for American participation in the United Nations, laying diplomatic groundwork despite initial isolationist opposition at home.

He worked to maintain American neutrality during the isolationist nineteen-thirties, but gradually built support for aid to Britain and the Soviet Union after 1941. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1945 for his role in founding the United Nations—the capstone to his lifelong commitment to international cooperation.

Franklin D. Roosevelt was the president under whom Hull served through depression and war. The United Nations was his lasting legacy; he shaped the vision of collective security and democratic governance that underpinned it. The Good Neighbor Policy was his reformulation of American relations with Latin America. And World War Two was the defining crisis of his tenure; he worked to align American interests with the Allies.
